messages.subject: Some specialized routines
messages.subject_clean: Some specialized routines
messages.body_plain:
I've written some routines to perform a small subset of what occu does and I'm looking for feedback.

Why do this if occu already does this?  The main reason is that the routines provide "exact" maximum likelihood estimates of psi and p with no iterative procedures needed (when the number of visits per site is constant and no larger than 4 visits per site).  I can see this having potential help for speeding up simulations and simply giving the ability to check on results from iterative procedures.

Only the basic model of occupancy is considered:  constant probability of presence, constant detection probability, and a common number of visits per site.  (In other words, no covariates.)  Exact results are produced for the number of visits no larger than 4 and a different iterative procedure than occu when the visits are 5 or more.  Essentially the ability to provide exact maximum likelihood solutions is to consider the two sufficient statistics:  the number of sites with no detections (n0) and the total number of detections (m).

I've attached two R files:  one with the routines (occu exact routines.r) and one (occu exact test.r) that shows an example as to how to run things.  I've also attached the equivalent code written in Wolfram Mathematica which allows you to use pull-down menus to select the required information:  number of sites (n), number of visits per site (v), number of sites with no detections (n0), and the total number of detections (m).  Below is a screenshot of the Wolfram CDF document:

One can download the CDF reader for free at www.wolfram.com/cdf-player <http://www.wolfram.com/cdf-player>.  It's a large file but you only have to install it once.  (Disclaimer:  I do not officially endorse any products.)

I also have similar code for exact Bayesian estimates but it was suggested by a couple of wise folks that you all know to start by sharing some of the code here.  Please let me know if this is of any use or if you have any suggestions.

Thanks,

Jim

I am running bird models in gdistsamp and am also encountering this issue when trying to run parboot.  I have a top model that looks great (standardized covs, simulations look good), but at some point in the parboot, a sim doesn't work, gets an "error in optim", then the parboot stops.  Ideally, I'm trying to run 100 sims, but I've managed to lower the number of sims for a couple of species (50 or 75 sims) and eventually it will run all the way through so I get my GoF stat. Richard Schuster (or anyone!), would you be willing to walk me through the "try" code??

Many thanks in advance for any help, and I'm happy to post/send code as needed.
Melissa Roach

Hi all,

This Group has been a huge help to me as I’ve attempted to learn unmarked—thanks to everyone who devotes time to helping folks like me.  Here’s the problem that finally spurred me to post a question:

I have distance sampling data for breeding birds from 140 point count stations that were surveyed four times during the breeding season.  Temporary emigration models (Chandler et al. 2011) seemed ideal for these data, but after a lot of attempts, I’ve decided to not model availability.  I have a good idea of true density from intensive territory mapping for one species of interest, but model estimates for that species are more than twice the “true” density.  The reason for this, I believe, is that replicate counts in this system (desert grasslands) vary widely in detections, which results in low estimates of phi (mean <0.5) despite any survey-level (“yearly site-level” in gdistsamp) covariates that I include.

Instead, my approach until recently was to sum the detections from all surveys for each distance class and include an offset of the number of surveys in distsamp models.  Although I’ve never been confident about this approach, the estimates seem reasonable, and I have good model fit for most species.  After reading pertinent chapters in the new Kery and Royle and playing with the yellow wagtail data, I decided to try stacking my data and using gdistsamp on unmarked frames with no yearlySiteCovs.  This is appealing because it would allow me to try negative binomial mixtures and model survey-level covariates on the detection function.  I suspected that if I fit two models with the same abundance and detection covariates: 1) a distsamp model with summed data and an offset, and 2) a gdistsamp model with stacked data and no yearlySiteCovs, estimates would be very similar.  Sure enough, these two models returned identical parameter estimates and SEs.  The problem arises, however, when I run GOF tests on these two models.  Fit statistics for the distsamp model look good, but for the gdistsamp model, results are abysmal.

So this brings me to two questions:

1) Are there any obvious problems with my approach that are glaringly obvious?

2) If not, why are the fit statistics from two models with identical parameter estimates and SEs so different?

Hopefully, I’m just being dense and missing something obvious, but figuring it out seems to be beyond me at this point.  Below are some simplified code and outputs that (maybe) make this more clear.  I tried to alter the wagtail data a bit to reproduce my problem, but it seems that I can’t get a Poisson mixture with only site-level covariates (which I need to demonstrate my distsamp/offset approach) to return decent fit statistics.

 Marc and I are writing a chapter on the famous "Dail-Madsen" model for the Volume 2 of the AHM book.  One issue that we've stumbled up against and simply cannot resolve is to get the DM model running in WinBUGS or JAGS when there are some covariate effects on some of the model parameters (this runs in unmarked using the pcountOpen function).

 In any case, I'm offering this problem up to the community to see if someone can solve the problem. IF you can get this running in WinBUGS or JAGS (or OpenBUGS for that matter) in a reasonable consistent way, for covariates on some of the model parameters, then you will get a free copy of Volume 2 when it comes out (or V. 1 if you wish). Plus you get a huge thanks and acknowledgement in the book!

In addition if someone can take the script below and provide a NIMBLE implementation, also free book for that!  We may use NIMBLE in vol 2 ....

 Below is a simple script which consists of a data simulator function where you provide the basic parameters including covariate effects for each parameter. Then after that is a bit of code to write out the BUGS model and call JAGS to try to fit it. In the example below we try to run it (but fail) with a covariate effect only on "lambda" (initial abundance), although covariate effects are simulated for all 4 model parameters. Recall that the Dail-Madsen model has 4 basic parameters: initial abundance (lambda), survival (phi), recruitment (gamma) and detection probability (p).

 JAGS always fails on the dreaded "inconsistent node" error. It seems impossible to choose decent starting values for this model....

 Note that the DM model simulator has 2 distinct recruitment models :  "absolute" and "per capita" as we note them in the BUGS file. Neither of those work.

 Note 2: the model works fine without covariate effects (I can send that script if you want to see it).

 Note 3: It's possible that the parameter values we use here are such nonsense that it's impossible to satisfy them. If anyone has some ideas on that which resolve the problem, then that counts as a win.

 Note 4: There could be errors in our code below and if you find some you only get the prize if the model runs!

 To claim your prize, just post a solution to this problem with any BUGS engine or NIMBLE that works if I run it.

Thanks all!
regards
andy

DMsimv2.fn <- function(M = 50, J = 3, T = 5, mean.lambda = 4, mean.gamma.rel = 0.5, mean.phi = 0.8, mean.p = 0.7, beta.lam = 1, beta.gamma = 1, beta.phi = -1, beta.p = -1){
# Simulation for multiple-visit data,
# constant time intervals between primary periods
# M: Number of sites
# J: Number of replicate (secondary) samples within period of closure
# T: Number of primary samples: years, seasons etc.
# mean.lambda: Initial expected abundance at cov.lam = 0
# mean.gamma.rel, mean.phi: recruitment and apparent survival rates,
#   respectively, at values of cov.gamma and cov.phi equal to 0
# mean.p: detection probability at cov. p = 0
# beta.X is the slope of parameter X (link transformed) on the respective covariate
y <- p <- array(NA, dim = c(M, T, J))
N <- matrix(NA, M, T)
S <- R <- matrix(NA, M, T-1)
cov.lam <- runif(M, -1, 1)
cov.gamma <- runif(M, -1, 1)
cov.phi <- runif(M, -1, 1)
cov.p <- array(runif(M*T*J, -1, 1), dim = dim(y))
logit<- function(x){ log(x/(1-x)) }

lambda <- exp(log(mean.lambda) + beta.lam * cov.lam)
N[,1] <- rpois(M, lambda)        # Initial state

phi <- plogis(logit(mean.phi) + beta.phi * cov.phi)
gamma <- exp(log(mean.gamma.rel) + beta.gamma * cov.gamma)

for(t in 1:(T-1)) {              # State dynamics
   S[,t] <- rbinom(M, N[,t], phi)
   R[,t] <- rpois(M, N[,(t)]*gamma)    # Simulate in 'relative' mode
   N[,t+1] <- S[,t] + R[,t]
}
for(i in 1:M){                   # Observation process
   for(t in 1:T){
      for(j in 1:J){
         p[i,t,j] <- plogis(logit(mean.p) + beta.p * cov.p[i,t,j])
         y[i,t,j] <- rbinom(1, N[i,t], p[i,t,j])
      }
   }
}

# Put observed data into two dimensions
yy <- ccov.p <- array(NA, dim = c(M, J*T))
for(t in 1:T){
   yy[,(J * t-(J-1)):(J*t)] <- y[,t,]
   ccov.p[,(J * t-(J-1)):(J*t)] <- cov.p[,t,]
}
# Output
return(list(M = M, J = J, T = T, mean.lambda = mean.lambda, mean.gamma.rel = mean.gamma.rel, mean.phi = mean.phi, mean.p = mean.p, beta.lam = beta.lam, beta.gamma = beta.gamma, beta.phi = beta.phi, beta.p = beta.p, cov.lam = cov.lam, cov.gamma = cov.gamma, cov.phi = cov.phi, cov.p = cov.p, ccov.p = ccov.p, N = N, S = S, R = R, p = p, y = y, yy = yy))
}

set.seed(24)
data <- DMsimv2.fn(M = 50, J = 3, T = 5, mean.lambda = 4, mean.gamma.rel = 0.5, mean.phi = 0.8, mean.p = 0.7, beta.lam = 1,
 beta.gamma = 1, beta.phi = -1, beta.p = -1)
str(data)

# Bundle data
win.data <- list(C = data$y, M = dim(data$y)[1], J = dim(data$y)[3], T = dim(data$y)[2], cov.lam = data$cov.lam)
, cov.gamma = data$cov.gamma, cov.phi = data$cov.phi, cov.p = data$ccov.p)

# Specify model in BUGS language
cat(file = "DM2.txt","
model {
# Priors
alpha.lam <- logit(mean.lambda)
mean.lambda ~ dunif(0, 100)    # Population growth rate
gamma ~ dunif(0, 5)            # per-capita recruitment rate
phi ~ dunif(0, 1)              # apparent survival (omega in paper/unmarked)
p ~ dunif(0, 1)                # Detection probability

beta ~ dnorm(0,0.1)

# Likelihood
for(i in 1:M){
   # State process: initial condition
   N[i,1] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
   log(lambda[i]) <- alpha.lam + beta * cov.lam[i]
   # State process: transition model
   for(t in 1:(T-1)){
     S[i,t+1] ~ dbin(phi, N[i,t])
     R[i,t+1] ~ dpois(gamma)           # 'absolute' recruitment = 'constant'
   #  tmp[i,t] <- N[i,t] * gamma      # per-capita recruitment = 'autoreg'
   #  R[i,t+1] ~ dpois(tmp[i,t])  # per-capita recruitment = 'autoreg'
     N[i,t+1] <- S[i,t+1] + R[i,t+1]
   }

# Observation process
   for(t in 1:T){
      for(j in 1:J){
         C[i,t,j] ~ dbin(p, N[i,t])
      }
   }
}

# Derived quantities: N for selected sites
}
")

# Initial values
R1 <- apply(data$y, c(1,2), max) # Use observed max. counts + 2 or even bigger as inits for recruitment
R1[,1] <- NA
N1 <- R1   # Initial population size
N1[,1:data$T] <- NA
N1[,1] <- apply(apply(data$y, c(1,2), max), 1, max)+1
inits <- function(){list(phi = 0.8, gamma=0.5, p=0.7, mean.lambda = 4, N = N1, R = R1+2, beta = 1)}

# Parameters monitored
params <- c("mean.lambda", "beta", "gamma", "phi", "p")
# params <- c("lambda", "gamma", "phi", "p", "N")

# MCMC settings

ni <- 10000   ;   nt <- 1   ;   nb <- 5000   ;  nc <- 3

library(jagsUI)
# Call JAGS from R
system.time(out2 <- jags(win.data, inits, params, "DM2.txt", n.chains = nc, n.thin = nt, n.iter = ni, n.burnin = nb))

print(out2, 3)

p ~ dunif(0, 1)                # Detection probability

beta ~ dnorm(0,0.1)

   # State process: initial condition
   N[i,1] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
   log(lambda[i]) <- alpha.lam + beta * cov.lam[i]
   # State process: transition model
   for(t in 1:(T-1)){
     S[i,t+1] ~ dbin(phi, N[i,t])

#     R[i,t+1] ~ dpois(gamma)           # 'absolute' recruitment = 'constant'

     tmp[i,t] <- N[i,t] * gamma      # per-capita recruitment = 'autoreg'

     R[i,t+1] ~ dpois(tmp[i,t])  # per-capita recruitment = 'autoreg'
     N[i,t+1] <- S[i,t+1] + R[i,t+1]
   }

# Observation process
   for(t in 1:T){
      for(j in 1:J){
         C[i,t,j] ~ dbin(p, N[i,t])
      }
   }
}

# Derived quantities: N for selected sites

")

I don't quite follow the reduction from 162 to 23 (is 162 the total # visits? Not sure how this is being fit), but I might stick with the Poisson mixture.   G-o-f indicates the Poisson mixture barely over-dispersed. A very low value of c-hat may also indicate lack of fit, and I think that maybe this is the case with the NB here. As a note, it is generally best to estimate c-hat using a full model to ensure that the model set includes a suitable candidate.  Using  G-o-f  assessments of  a null model to compare mixture distributions is problematic: if there is any real ecological variance, the NB null model should generally perform far better than the Poisson null model.

The AHM book (chapter 6) has a useful section on issues with the Negative Binomial mixture often providing better 'fit' or goodness of fit, and poorer prediction, and there have been several papers that have discussed NB vs. ZIP, e.g., Joseph et al. 2009 Modeling abundance using N-mixture models: the importance of considering ecological mechanisms , in Ecologial Applications.

Dear Rob,

I agree with John and would use the Poisson mixture, which in terms of AIC is barely worse than the NB and seems to have hardly any overdispersion. I believe that at worst, you will underestimate abundance when using a Poisson where in fact you should use something allowing for more overdispersion. Usually, people would be OK with having a more 'conservative' assessment of the 'health' of a population, i.e., knowing that there are probably at least as many animals as the Poisson Nmix says.

I know that all this may seem a little unsatisfactory. I would use the NB if you really have (in terms of GoF) but ONLY when the resulting abundance estimates pass the commonsense GoF test, i.e., do not predict something outragously high.

As we said in the AHM book, we think that more research is needed here to better understand how the NB model can sometimes be vastly preferred by GoF and yet predict unrealistic abundance levels.

G-o-f indicates the Poisson mixture barely over-dispersed. A very low value of c-hat may also indicate lack of fit, and I think that maybe this is the case with the NB here. As a note, it is generally best to estimate c-hat using a full model to ensure that the model set includes a suitable candidate.  Using  G-o-f  assessments of  a null model to compare mixture distributions is problematic: if there is any real ecological variance, the NB null model should generally perform far better than the Poisson null model.

The AHM book (chapter 6) has a useful section on issues with the Negative Binomial mixture often providing better 'fit' or goodness of fit, and poorer prediction, and there have been several papers that have discussed NB vs. ZIP, e.g., Joseph et al. 2009 Modeling abundance using N-mixture models: the importance of considering ecological mechanisms , in Ecologial Applications.

Cheers,

John

messages.body_plain:
Hi Auriel,

For gdistsamp, getP returns the interval-specific detection probability, conditional on an individual begin available for detection. As with most other distance sampling methods (and if the individual is available for detection), detection probability is assumed to be 1 when distance=0. However, detection probability for the first interval will be less than 1 because it is the average detection probability of individuals in that interval.

Hope that helps.

Richard
